review:
This really felt more like an experience than a game, the story was absolutely amazing! Night City is one of the best open worlds I've ever played, and the amount of detail put into it, and even the lore around the world and characters of Cyberpunk itself was insane. The RPG elements also make you have to take your decisions seriously throughout the story, because it really doesn't hold back, and that's one of the main things that gives it such a unique tone and atmosphere.

Highly recommended! 10/10

[h1] Cyberpunk 2077 review [/h1]

First off I want to say that I didnt get have to endure the incredible buggy and broken State it came out with, which must have been a bummer to some people eager to finally play in and expierience the world of Cyberpunk 2077.

But after about 5 Years the developers finally had enough time to pull through and eliminate mostly all the bugs and issues that the game started with. And thats where I bought it. 


[h3] Graphics [/h3]
[list]
[*]Just like imagined - perfectly fit for depicting the worlds narrative and capitalist nightmare futurism, sadly at the cost of your fps - Good specs recommended to be able to expierience the beauty of high graphics settings. (or mods to make it even more beautiful)
[*]detailed where it needs to be
[*]nighttime rain is incredible
[*]realistic character skin 
[/list]


[h3] Gameplay [/h3]

[list] 
[*]many builds to try (just be careful to think about it [b] before [/b] upgrading the perk tree you cant reset it infinite amount of times
[*]cyberware is amazing, though some slots in the body are reserved for only one type of (recommended) build path 
[*]many sidequests you can either stumble into or get them marked on the map, less story relevant more detailled look at the people around you. Often many shards with text to get a context of the situation your put into.
[*]the dialoge options are well thought through and aren't cryptic for the most parts of the game, sometimes they are locked through amount of points spend in the skill tree on a specific skill
[*]Gunplay is satisfying especially the unique weapons are really worthwhile trying out, the default weapons kinda all feel the same in their respective category, with winners mostly being the ones with the best stats
[*]Movement is almost limitless, you can scale buildings all you want, get a whole new angle on the mission you are on, barbed wire is a bit iffy sometimes
[*]Fast travel only unlocks the option when you have been to the spot at least once already, in the city fast travel isnt as cool as driving through it anyways (in the outlands it can be a bit boring to drive)
[*]Vehicles are working as intended, some have weapons build into some you can only find in the world or be given as a reward. If you call a vehicle to you (especially with cars) there is a bug with slopes that makes their spawn a bit weird and they either spawn too high in the air and fall down or too low in the ground and shoot out of the ground but its not as often as on release
[*]scanning in missions is used often and I understand that but sometimes it just takes too long for my liking
[*]hacking is well thought through and hacking through cameras and vehicles also makes it a good tool to mark enemy positions and a path you want to go if your not full intelligence build 
[*]modding is made accessible and easy to do with things like Vortex mod manager, there are many mods to explore (flying vehicles!) just be careful to keep the 18+ filter on lol 
[/list]

[h3] Story [/h3]


I wont be spoiling much of the story so I keep it short in this one

[list] [*]main game story good and has 5 endings to explore, one of them being secret and all of them are peak (the phone calls you get are soul shattering)
[*]the Phantom Liberty dlc was outstanding story wise, throwing you into a full blown secret agent-esque story within dogtown (located at the big stadium next to pacifica). There are 4 endings to explore and they broke me even more then the main story endings. [/list]


[h2] conclusion [/h2]


Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game with great gameplay, it is absolutely worth every cent (especially with discount). CD PROJECT RED thankfully managed to turn the buggy mess of 2020 into a fully fleshed out masterpiece with hunderts of hours of playtime possibilities. I got captured by the story and the characters. I think so much discussion at release focused on what a steaming pile of trash this game's code was that it distracted from both the good and the bad. As I finally visit this game with a complete playthrough well over 5 years later, with I suppose a good chunk of the problems fixed, I can weigh in objectively having never played this game at release time.

First, this game is still horrifically buggy. People who say that the problems have been fixed are grading this on a curve versus the original release. Leaving the room where I flatlined the voodoo guy via the blackwall, I would, for example, be frozen in place while crouching and scope focused while stepping on a bit of conduit on the floor. That simple movement is still unsolved in some cases is glaring. I'm not going to go through all the bugs, just that this is still at a point that the problems are completely immersion breaking and required me to redo from saves many times.

Secondly, Keanu Reeves is a horrifically unsuited for his role here. It was a cheap and tawdry way to promote the game to cast him as Johnny. Keanu excels when he can play someone who is completely overcome by awe (The Matrix) or a stoned idiot (Bill and Ted). These are some of my favorite movies. I don't hate him as an actor. But let's face it, he should be typecasted into a very specific kind of role which is not Johnny. Keanu Reeves cannot play an emotionally stagnant revolutionary displaced decades into the future. This role is much too nuanced for him, and his voice bits come off as overread and contrived in the manner of a high school theater production. It's embarrassing. This comes off to me as cheap PR that compromises the work. Which is sad, because there are many characters here that are so well acted and could have created a timeless emotive experience that was beloved as Skyrim, but they are overshadowed by Johnny's piss-poor dialogue reading.

Anyways, the game is good enough. Play it.

First time playing Cyberpunk? Buy it, install it, and prepare to go on a trip. 

This game blends stealth, technical, and even guns blazing gameplay incredibly well. I ran around pinging "Short Circuit" on everyone on Normal Difficulty, but the game REALLY got fleshed out when I went on the harder difficulties. Still, I recommend "Normal" if it's your first time as a merc in Night City. Go ham.

Returning to Cyberpunk? Reinstall it, and play it on "Hard" or "VERY HARD". Mods optional but recommended.

Like your other "build" games like Fallout, the higher the difficulty the more important it is to spec into a build. It makes progression feel significantly better as your cyberware really does build up, and the game WILL kick your butt until you reach that stage. Become a Netrunner that kills before anyone else sees you, or a Desperado from Metal Gear Rising with some heavy & sharp Mantis Blades.

For example, I set out for a "Gorilla Arms" build and at first I had to draw out Cyberpsychos from their den so I could run them over with my car. I went from just grabbing whatever gun could make me that money I needed for those sweet new implants to going full Donkey Kong on some mad fools, throwing their comrades around like barrels off a crimson girder.

Either way, be ready to hit the big leagues, choom. And be sure to pay back Victor.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that has made me think long and hard about a lot of things. It's an incredible setting and a fantastically presented world. After the fixes they made to the game on release (which i had the privilege not to play), it feels smooth as butter to play, and it felt incredibly rewarding to master the game through multiple playthroughs.

To sing more praises, the phantom liberty expansion gave me a deeply rewarding story experience and an addition onto an already very fun game.

Unfortunately however, it does have its flaws, and to be frank near all of them have to do with the main story. I take issue with how the setup to the game, one where you're dying, is not at all conducive to an immersive experience if you want to go off and do side objectives. I also think that Johnny Silverhand is a misogynist who is never properly made to reckon with his actions, and particularly playing as female V, one of Johnny's quests later on (Chippin' in) feels immensely uncomfortable and violating.

Overall i'd say I'd recommend the game, but given it has flaws that are extremely difficult to ignore (given one of them literally lives inside V's head) i'd give it a 7/10 or so.

Their generic nature clashes with the high quality of the rest. At least it doesn't hurt to ignore them - but it would be better, if everything in a game would be fun to do.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best success stories for a game that started off rocky for many people, but managed to update significantly for all platforms until it reached the proper standards for CD Projekt Red that's expected after the Witcher 3. 

Personally, as someone who never knew anything Cyberpunk related until playing this game, it made me invested and hooked into learning more about the overall lore of the world outside of playing. The uniqueness of the entire setting of Cyberpunk dystopia is an enjoyable playground to have in 2077.

The amount of power that you have over the way your character (V) is portrayed with a skillset that matches your playstyle is one of the most enjoyable experiences I've had in gaming. Starting off with barely being able to win a fistfight, to quite literally having gorilla arms attached to your character that lets you beat an entire gang hideout with your fists. Or, maybe you're more interested in a stealth profile with sniper rifles and hacking into anyone with cyberware in the game. 

There are just so many ways that you can enjoy this title from a gameplay perspective and even a graphical standpoint. It's one of the most beautiful games you can play on modern PC's, with probably the best usage of Ray Tracing in any current video game that makes 3000-4000+ series of Nvidia cards reach their actual potential. Photo mode was a welcome addition to capturing some of the best vistas or atmospheres that you can find in the lively Nightcity. 

Without getting into any spoilers, my only disappointment with the game that never was addressed was the lack of influence your background actually gives your character throughout the game. Sure, you'll be prompted with some dialogue that your background allows you to answer differently or find a way around skillchecks, but in terms of consistent missions or things that allow you to "roleplay" your V to potential simply are non existent. Act One of the game should've been more focused on your actual background and should've been longer overall so players could experience the importance of their background. 

Despite that flaw, I cannot find many others with the game at this point. You play it and get lost for hours at a time from how much nightcity sucks you in. Everytime you finish a mission or a bounty, you'll tell yourself "just one more" and before you know it, it's midnight. The impressive audio rivals games like GTA V and some modern FPS with quality that goes above and beyond. 

I would recommend this game to anyone at full price, especially on sale, and find yourself an RPG that lives up to the standard set by games like Skyrim over a decade ago. The post-game support (even adding an expansion) shows the TLC that the devs had for reaching their vision for the game. I'm happy to say they redeemed themselves and Cyberpunk from it's horrendous launch.

The game run on average 30-45 FPS on a potato laptop with Medium to High settings (Low Crowd Density), i'll say it's good performance wise if you are gaming on the budget like me. 

as for the game itself, i think i will give it 8/10,
PROS:
- It's fun to run around as Netrunner in Night City, but after several hours i kinda feel that the game is kinda too easy, maybe my decision making a Netrunner V is have a big role on it too.

- The world itself feels big and lively (even at low crowd settings),
 
- The story is good enough to keep me playing, especially Phantom Liberty DLC part, i think the Relic mechanic it introduce is really fun, and Tower Ending (without Spoiler) might be the best ending of all time in my opinion. I would say though, after you watch some in-game news on tv, you probably will be like me and think "wow, the world building in this game is kinda fun and chaotic".

- CDPR also have make mod support for the games, making it kinda easy to add mods, especially for stuff like tiny immersion fixes, you know, the unnecessary detail like making all in game ads fully animated or pettable cat (yes you can adopt cat and iguana in this game, weirdly enough, you can only pat the iguana, still, they are both cute though).

- also, the music are awesome, if you have watched Edgerunner on Netflix, you might already have taste a little bit of those juicy bangers. but let me tell you, most of the songs in this games are really good. Recently, i even start to make a habbit of listening to some of the songs while doing chores, especially Chippin In, Pon Pon Sh*t (Jhonny Silverhand version, it's easter egg, not in Radio) and Never Fade Away, they really make me forgot how exhausting doing daily laundry was. (FYI, most of the songs from anime are in Body Heat Radio btw, including that song).

- Easter eggs, lots of easter eggs, really fun. I kinda don't want to talk too much about this because it was really fun if you notice something you don't know, but just you know, there are a lot of eater egg in this game. (just so you know, Murkman is the best detective)

CONS:
-Even though most of annoying bug from first released was already been patched and fixed, there are still some minor bug or glitches in the game, Some like driving drift, texture pop-in (not as bad as first released) and that one time Jackie walk through lockers during the first mission are might tied to FPS and you machine, but stuff like auto drive feature driver recklesly or showing negative million numbers (it was without mod btw) and monowire doesn't glow at all sometimes are still small stuff that need fixes in my opinion. (also, i know Fream gen is bad since it will give you low latency, but so far, i can't use frame gen at all. It will crash on me when i open map, even when using the settings for RTX 30s and 20s, so i don't know what kind of stuff that will happened if you able to use it on RTX 20s or 30s).

- lack of consequences might be one factor that make the story can feel a bit monotone and less exciting for me. Like, don't get me wrong, some dialogue choice does lock you out from good reward, like when i miss my chance to get Jackie guns for free, but like what i just said, "for free", mean you don't really missing out much when you make a wrong choices, if you own the DLC you can just buy your best friend's gun from the vendor in Dogtown. pretty neat since it was your best friend's gun, you know something that supposed to be sentimental for his family and people close by :). And not only that, if you fail to save someone who will give you car if you save them, you can also just,,, buy the car. Yeah, no sh*t i actually kinda lost excitement when i find out i can just buy stuff i missed out, like, i might get that some stuff like buying car from someone being killed in street race kinda make sense, but buying your own best friend's gun? I don't think Mama Wells or Misty will appreciate me to buy item that so sentimental for them (it kinda make me feels like paying people to make myself a grave robber). And it's just about rewards, you can try to just never talk when the timer is on during dialogue, there are some exception that instant kill you, but most of them at least from my experience, you don't really need to do anything to resolve the situation. As a big fan of the Witcher 3, I went into Cyberpunk 2077 with high expectations, but I can definitely say that those expectations were met. The combat system is also very flexible with many different weapon types and cyberware options for all sorts of different builds, and the game features a nice variety of enemies you can test your skills on. I also thought the soundtrack and radio songs were great, and appreciated the excellent voice acting in the quests. My only complaint about the game is that although most of the bugs were fixed since its initial release, I still encountered a few crashes and weird glitches throughout the gameplay, some of which were pretty funny. Overall, I'd give this game a 9.5/10, definitely an incredible and memorable experience!

From the creators of Bloodyborne and Dark Souls, you essentially get a glorified dating sim that is confusedly also an open world RPG. The areas are vast and beautiful yet the main attractions remain the women in this game. You have Ranni the Witch. I don't need to tell you how popular she is. Let's just say 4373 is a large number for people dedicating "art posts" to her. Then you have Melina, your first maiden. That childhood friend/neighbor girl character who has been helping you along the way throughout out your quests and just waiting for you to notice her. Soft spoken yet meaningful in her words and easy on the eyes. Just don't show her the three fingers, she's not into that...Then you have Fia. The deathbed companion. The character you go to after dying to the boss over and over again. Why? Because if you can't feel the warmth of a woman's body in real life, might as well pretend to feel it in a triple AAA game from Miyazaki. And to maintain realism, whenever you hug her you get debuffed, just like how it feels to hug women in real life; it doesn't last long, its lackluster, and you keep coming back for more while losing your grip on reality. Then you have Hyetta. She's the gal with an appetite. Feed her some grapes and she'll be over the moon. Feed her enough, and she will show you her three fingers (pun intended). You also have the amazon goddess of snoo snoo herself, Nepheli...the one with daddy issues. I know Gideon said he "adopted her" but...cmon. The guy who is all knowing wouldn't know how to court a barbarian women? Really?. That aside, the cutest one...the tsundere that sets your heart on fire...Dung Eater-chan. I swear...his eyes are as brown as the left over basketball sized chocolate mud babies I leave in my toilet after a hearty Taco Bell breakfast. A character of rigour and personality. 

The characters are as diverse as the regions you play in. The weapons are unique and all usable up to end game. The only regret I have with this game is not being able to continually fight bosses like you could in Sekiro for example. That was a huge missed opportunity.

Elden Ring stands as a seminal achievement in interactive myth-making.

One thing this game does is encourage an approach to character progression. Whether you prefer the visceral, heavy-hitting cadence of a colossal sword or the distance of glintstone sorceries, the mechanical framework is amazing. As a "tarnished" which is sent into the world long after signifcant events occur, witnessing the aftermath of a war that fractured reality itself and creating a narrative depth it make the game feel both haunting and monumental.

A game that truly earns its title of GOTY and will undoubtedly remain a cherished masterpiece for many.

I remember hearing about Elden Ring for the first time in 2022. A lot of my friends hyped the game up as one of the greatest of all time. and ranted and raved about how innovative it was.  I had never played a "souls-like" game in my life and thus wasn't very interested. Fast forward to ~2024, I started to dip my toes in the genre. My first was a game called Mortal Shell. I liked it. Then I played through Sekiro (also from fromsoft) in 2025 but got hard-stuck on the final boss. 

In 2026, I decided to try Elden Ring for the first time. I bought it on sale for I think around 30 dollars. From the first couple hours, I was totally entranced by this game. My friends were not kidding - this game is legitimately a modern masterpiece.

The Pros:
The map is absolutely shockingly massive. The overworld map alone feels much larger than any other game I have ever played. And then you find out about the wells, and realize "â¥â¥â¥â¥â¥â¥â¥â¥â? It gets even bigger." Most games that have large maps have long stretches of barren, lifeless areas that artificially increase the size. Not Elden Ring. Not at all. EVERY area of the game is not only breath-takingly beautiful, but also filled to the brim with unique structures that even transform and change as you reach milestones in the game's story.

There are hundreds of unique enemies, mini-bosses, and bosses to fill in the aforementioned map. Exciting, challenging encounters lay waiting around every corner to be discovered by the player. You'll be walking through a dungeon, and all of a sudden - "WHOA WHAT THE F**K IS THAT THING" - you'll be attacked by an abomination. Skeletons. Lizards. Dragons, Worm people. Dogs. Crazy villagers. etc. Each enemy and boss has their own unique attacks and animations and it absolutely never gets old. It is a very refreshing change from most modern video games, that largely reuse the same "pool" of attacks and animations without really caring about the gameplay becoming boring.

What's the point of enemies without weapons, right? Good news - Elden Ring has hundreds of unique ones to choose from, most of which can be further modified with "ashes of war" found throughout the game. You want to wield a battle-axe that makes people bleed? Done. What about a sword that freezes enemies? Done. What about a giant hammer that poisons? Done. The customization is borderline limitless. And the armor in this game is largely the same way. There are tons of different sets to choose from or mix and match, that raise certain attributes to fit your particular playstyle. No matter how you want to play, this game has options for YOU which is awesome and shows they really deeply thought about the combat from an early stage of development.

The voice acting in this game is another thing I'd like to highlight. It is absolutely perfect. Every enemy. Every boss. Every NPC. There were many times during this game that the voice acting gave me chills - which is very rare  for me and especially in video games- such as mohg's "NIHIL! NIHIL! NIHIL!" or Godrick's "Forefathers one and all, bear witness!" This game FEELS like you as the player are actually living in this huge fantasy landscape. It's amazing.



The cons:
It pains me to really say anything negative about this game because I, like many others, consider it a legitimate modern masterpiece to gaming. However, with that being said, there are a few things I must critique.

The storyline, while there, certainly feels a little bit lacking to me. The developers absolutely give you bits and pieces of a story throughout the game but it is largely through experiencing the world and going to different areas. It feels a little bit disjointed and confusing at times.

Some particular bosses in this game have legitimate "Guaranteed hit" moves. It's a souls-like game, so of course there's going to be stuff like that and what I'm about to say isn't a "major" critique but remains true to me. I feel like a lot of bosses (particularly late game bosses) should be a little more choreographed than what they are. Some bosses are programmed to essentially do "random mix ups" meaning they can chain an attack with another attack or this other attack or this other attack. They essentially randomly pick from a set of moves. In theory this is cool, until you encounter a boss like Mohg, lord of blood or Malenia and then you want to smash your controller into bits and pieces. You are going to be hit by a lot of attacks that will have you going "wait a second, that wasn't even close to me wtf" and you aren't tripping. Some attacks really, literally, can look or feel as though they are clearly dodged and just.... aren't. On the flip-side, some attacks are virtually guaranteed regardless of how you want to dodge/roll. Malenia's "waterfowl dance" is a perfect example of this. Although *technically* dodge-able, if you are close to her when she does it? Son... It's over. There are memes online that say the best thing you can do when she does waterfowl close range is to just exit and try the run again until you get a tamer mix-up and lowkey?....... they're accurate LMFAO. I just really wish that wasn't the case. Your success, particularly in late-game bosses, often feels like you're just waiting for a fight where they don't do X attack or don't have such punishing mix-ups. The fight that I finally killed Malenia she only did waterfowl once in phase 2. There were other fights where she'd do it 4-5 times and again, if you get a fight like that (which mind you is rng) it is ACTUALLY just over unless you're a perfect god with thousands of hours on these types of games. Again, not a major critique because it's a souls-like game - just a personal preference. I like bosses that have more choreographed attacks. If this part is putting you off from trying this game - Don't worry! This game has lots of fights that are fairly choreographed and very fun!! There are only really 3-5 bosses in the whole game that I would consider just outright unfair in the sense that your success is literally just waiting for good rng. And believe me, when you run into them in your journey... you'll know. (lol)

My only other gripe with this game is how it does quests. I considered tying this part in with the storyline critique but my issue is with characters that aren't necessarily "needed" for the story and thus I feel it deserves it's own section. A lot of the quests in this game are - and I am not exaggerating in the slightest - Find X character here at random location on the map. Then talk to them and find them here in totally different area opposite side of the map. Then talk to them and find them here in this totally unrelated area of the map opposite to that. If you want to do a particular ending or just help particular npcs - you will 100% without a doubt need to search up how to do some things. I personally wanted to save Melina from her death and so I did Hyetta's questline. It was horrifically painful to experience before I succumbed to using google for help. Her questline in particular is absolute, total dogs*it so much so that it's actually unbelievable. Her questline involves an invisible door that you open with a pressure plate some place in a random dungeon on the map. For real. I am not exaggerating.(LMFAO) Remember how I said that you will need google for certain parts? I really mean that. I don't think it is actually possible as a solo player to find certain things without it. And I got to say - that right there is my biggest critique about this game. Even if the developers included vague dialogue like  "I'm going to the mountains of ____" or something just to give the player a general idea of where to look for them to advance their quest would be all they would need to do to fix this. 

All in all, Elden Ring is an absolutely INCREDIBLE game. Despite having a few cons, I believe the pros vastly outweigh them. It is one of the best games of all time, and I would have paid double full price if I had known.

I mean: Why would the most powerful wizard ever - Merlin - secretly build dozens of hidden gazebos all over the place waiting to be revealed by a bored enough magic student, who has nothing better to do than to solve some of the simplest puzzles one by one? Well, never mind...

Campaign will cost you about 40 hours (or less, if you're speed running) to finish, plus the sidequests, the challenges and achievements another 40 hours. Definitely a must for Harry Potter fans, the details are true to the lore and nearly accurate. Sophronia Franklin's quiz will surely measure your knowledge of the Wizarding world lore (I did not get any single one correct in the difficult round). All achievements are casually easy to get, except the secret ones wherein you'll have to play until near mid-game on every house. (to which, the differences between instances for different houses, the story differs. After discovering your goal is where all stories connect, whatever House you have chosen). If you want to see Azkaban for a brief moment, then I suggest Hufflepuff as your house, as it features a visit to the said place. The combat is superbly engaging. 
Only drawbacks on the game:
 - Blue characters: This is not a bug but a feature, though it sometimes activates automatically (just turn off High Contrast Gameplay, under accessibility Options)
 - Flashing lights, white flickering: This commonly happens during in-game daytime, and when entering enclosed spaces (houses, caves, underground tunnels), commonly caused by enabling "Frame Generation" on PC, issues with ray tracing, or memory overload. (just turn off Frame Generation, toggling off Ray Tracing, updating GPU drivers, or disabling G-Sync. or just simply restart the game when it happens)
Overall, a marvelous representation to JK Rowling's Wizarding World.

Hogwarts Legacy is basically a "choose your own adventure" book if the only adventure you wanted was to be a magical menace. You start as a fifth-year student which is great because you skip the years of being a loser who can't do magic, and instead, you just show up on day one ready to throw hands with goblins and trolls. It's exactly like the movies, except instead of Harry Potter crying about his parents, it's you running around the castle at 3:00AM breaking into people's bedrooms to steal their loose change.

The best part is that the school rules are basically nonexistent. You can spend your afternoon "rescuing" magical beasts (which is really just shoving a giant purple toad into a magic suitcase) and then go straight to a dark forest to blast spiders into dust. The professors are like, "Don't go into the forbidden forest, it's dangerous!" and then five minutes later they're teaching you a spell that literally explodes someone?? The logic is hilarious, you're a fifteen year old kid wandering the place alone, taking out entire camps of dark wizards, and then you just stroll back into Herbology class to pet a screaming plant like nothing happened.

And let's talk about the combat. It"s way more satisfying than it has any right to be. You're flipping people upside down, setting them on fire, and slamming them into the dirt like a magical WWE wrestler. It's the ultimate wizard power trip, and honestly, the castle is so pretty I spent like three hours just walking into walls and looking at the paintings. 9/10, despite it all, it's a bit expensive.

Not since Trevor from GTA 5 have I played a character as vile and irredeemable as the protagonist in Hogwarts Legacy. And that is just by playing normally. 

Oh, the evil that I've wrought upon this world!

First, there's the main story, where I help my fellow wizards put down a wholly justified goblin uprising. After suffering generations of endless, racist oppression at the hands of wizards, a small, desperate band of freedom fighters are finally taking a heroic stand against the tyranny. Goblins in the Hogwarts universe aren't the monsters depicted in Tolkien's Middle Earth. Far from it. Goblins here are a race of intelligent, honest and hardworking artisans. Yet their greatest works of art are taken by wizards, never to be returned, while their communities are subjugated by a wizard-first class system that places goblins not much higher than house elves, and aims to keep them there. And even then, there are many goblins who refuse to take up arms and join the long-overdue uprising: a testament to their noble, peace-loving nature, which unfortunately for them is a quality that xenophobic wizards like me take advantage of at every opportunity. I'll kill every goblin that crosses my path for their inexcusable crime of wanting equality.

But I'm not satisfied with merely fighting to protect and preserve anti-goblin apartheid. Between quests, I take time off from my abject bigotry to turn my scumbaggery upon my own kind.

I spend a lot of time breaking and entering, busting house locks and stealing villagers' life savings. No one in Hogsmead (or anywhere for that matter) is safe from my wanton acts of vandalism and theft. I think I even stole someone's pajamas once!

But that's just the tip of the iceberg. I also hunt and kill people who are so poor, so desperate for a meal that they've taken to poaching in the Forbidden Forest, risking becoming meals themselves to the many foul creatures that lurk there just so that they can survive another day, and perhaps send some money home to their starving families. These poachers are not "dark wizards" no matter what label the affluent choose to stain them with. They are fathers, mothers, sons and daughters just trying to live another day. It's no wonder the Ministry of Magic turns a blind eye to their supposed crimes. But I don't, for I am a bloodthirsty psychopathic killer who delights in the agonized screams of my victims. I stalk these destitute people and murder them for sport in the most brutal, sadistic ways possible. I tear them apart; I set them ablaze; I throw carnivorous cabbages at them! For the infinitesimally small amount of coin that they may have, I act as judge, jury and executioner, where the only sentence is death... for poaching! Seriously, who does that?! Me. That's who.

I am pedigree wizard trash in this game. I suspect most Death Eaters have higher moral standards than me. But nobody can stop my path of destruction, for even without horcruxes I've already conquered death by using a dark spell called "Trya Gain" which resurrects me every time I die.

[h1] Hogwarts Legacy [/h1]

As a massive Harry Potter fan since I was a kid, jumping into this game for the first time was an absolute dream. Even though my first playthrough was on a much worse PC back when it launched, the sheer magic of exploring the world of this game kept me completely hooked. However, now that the initial hype has settled and I've put serious hours into it, my thoughts are a bit more grounded.

[h2] Positives [/h2]

The game offers an incredibly detailed and massive recreation of Hogwarts and the surrounding highlands. It feels like the ultimate realization of what fans have wanted for years, completely packed with secrets, landmarks, and collectibles to track down.

The magic system is another high point, featuring a diverse and rewarding combat loop. Fights stay engaging because you constantly unlock new spells that naturally expand your combos and tactical options as you progress.

On top of that, the progression loops feel meaningful, making you actually feel like a student growing into a powerful wizard. You unlock tools that dynamically grant access to earlier locked regions, which pairs nicely with excellent gear customization and a customizable Room of Requirement.

Finally, the cast of side characters is surprisingly well realized. Most companions have interesting backstories and unique personalities, and the narrative writing for their specific questlines is actually solid (e.g. Sebastian's lore). 

[h2] Negatives [/h2]

The biggest issue is the massive amount of open-world filler. The map is crowded with repetitive tasks that quickly become tedious chores, which ruins the pacing for anyone trying to clear all the side content.

Combat balance also completely breaks down by the late game. Healing items, combat potions, and the dark arts are so absurdly overtuned that they remove all challenge from major encounters, especially once you upgrade your talents.

This balance issue is made worse by the lack of mechanical variety in boss fights. Most unique targets and named foes are just standard enemy types with inflated health bars rather than bosses with distinct phases or mechanics.

There are also glaring lore breaks that hurt immersion. You can openly cast unforgivable curses in front of classmates and professors during main missions, and the world just completely ignores it.

To wrap it up, the main story ends on a flat note. The conclusion fails to acknowledge the weight of your choices or show how your journey impacted your friends after the credits roll.

[h2] Bugs & Performance [/h2]

I noticed heavy stuttering and frame drops inside the castle when moving between loading zones and walking through specific corridors, no matter what graphics settings I used. 

I also ran into a frustrating progression glitch, likely tied to Steam. Despite hitting 100% completion on my main save, a handful of achievements refused to unlock until I rebooted the application over a dozen times and spent a few hours troubleshooting. They all just triggered randomly at the exact same moment.

[h2] Content & Replay Value [/h2]

My playthroughs clocked in at roughly 90 hours on Hard difficulty, which included taking my time to hunt down around 90% of the hidden collectibles and finishing the optional storylines. Because the narrative path and choices are completely linear, there is almost no replay value here unless you are strictly trying to clean up missed achievements. 

[h2] Verdict: Good [/h2]

This is easily the finest title ever created for the Harry Potter universe, but it falls short of being a true masterpiece. While long-time fans will definitely find plenty to love, the experience is weighed down by generic open-world design and technical flaws.

Is it worth buying? Yes, it is a great experience for fans of the franchise, but I highly recommend grabbing it on a sale.

The whole time I was playing the game, I couldn't shake the feeling that the design team had created a beautiful world of Hogwarts and then just handed it off to the rest of the studio, who had no idea how and what to fill it with.

[h3]CONS:[/h3]
[u]The Story[/u] is very primitive. You're good, go fight evil. There are no dilemmas. Starting somewhere in the middle of the game, I just started skipping dialogues (especially in side quests) because they were boring and about nothing.

[u]An RPG without choices.[/u] No matter what you do, you have no influence on the story or the game world. Even when you clear out an enemy camp, after a while the enemies reappear there. Or, for example, there was a quest that just made me laugh. I had to find a book that another student had taken. She said, win my 5-question quiz and then I'll give it to you. I failed all 5 questions and she gave me the book anyway. Moreover, she didn't even comment on it. It's just like there's a book there, go get it. [u]There's no logic throughout the game.[/u]

[u]The economy is terrible[/u], so you're stuck in a world with [u]stupid puzzles[/u] for longer. I don't understand the challenge system at all. Complete 20 of the same puzzles to expand your inventory, or find all the tokens to get a CLOTHES COSMETICS IN SINGLEPLAYER GAME. There's also a very [u]big problem with loot[/u]. There's too much of it, and it's mostly worse than your own, especially when you level it up.

And whoever came up with the [u]real-time system[/u] for potion brewing, resource gathering, etc. (like in mobile games) has reserved a place in hell for themselves,

[h3]PROS:[/h3]
As I said, it's the game [u]world design[/u]. The designers, artists, and programmers did a great job on the details.

[u]The gameplay is simple but spectacular[/u]. I didn't get tired after 50 hours, but I would have liked more depth, such as spells interacting with each other or using the environment in battles. In short, the battles lack tactics.

Well, [u]some aspects[/u] of the plot were still intriguing, and there was a bit of epicness.

[b]In conclusion[/b], this game gives me very strange feelings. I kind of liked it, but I regret wasting my time on it. I definitely won't be replaying it.

I really like monster hunter, and Wilds is a great game. Now, it doesn't have the mandatory G/Master rank expansion yet, but even high rank has been a lot of fun, at least for me. I spent time crafting every single low rank and high rank piece of equipment in the game, so that I'd have a reason to play more of the game. I would dedicate a lot more time to charm farming, but I got very lucky with the drops.

And with the initial positivity out of the way, it's time for the things I don't like: Artian weapons, hunter symbols, charm farming, monster health and performance.

Artian weapons are a nice callback, but it's a serious shame that they're pretty much the best weapons in the game. Monster weapons are still good, but a god-roll artian weapon is simply better for most weapons. Layered weapons (in high rank for the first time) do help alleviate the issue of artian weapons sometimes being ugly. And now with the title update coming out in december, they're apparently making artian weapons EVEN BETTER. So goodbye monster weapons (except hunting horn and the bowguns, most likely). 

Hunter symbols and charm farming are both very time consuming. To start off with charms (or talismans), the drop rates for rarity 8 charms are terrible. I got very very lucky with getting charms I wanted as a lance and greatsword main (one has guard 3, another has focus 3 and weakness exploit 1). Rarity 7 charms can still be good too, as I've had several usable ones drop. Rarity 6 charms are more niche. SO while they create a gameplay loop, I don't find it too enjoyable, especially with how tanky 9 star monsters are.
As for my complaint with hunter symbols, you simply need too many of them. To craft every piece of gear in the game, you need well over 1000 hunter symbols. Quests usually drop 1-3, so it sure does take a while. Of course, you don't need that many hunter symbols if you don't have a completionist goal like mine in mind, but still.

As for monster health.. We deal a lot more damage compared to previous titles. So monster health has to keep up. The issue is, health is increased no matter what the monster is like. Case and point: tempered gore magala. It has more health than iceborne fatalis, in high rank. And the fight of gore magala revolves around it moving around quickly and being really aggressive, so the health pool should be slightly lower to account for that design. Despite that, it's the highest in the game. Artificially inflated stats don't add difficulty for me, they add annoyance.

And as for performance, I will say, I don't play at absolute max graphics. Is the difference in a setting noticeable enough to ruin everything for me if I notice it? No? Then i lower it a bit. With that being said, I do have a fairly beefy PC now (started off with a not-so-beefy PC), so I haven't encountered many issues. That being said, other people do experience issues. So I can't say it's a-okay. Good to look out for.

All in all, Wilds is a great monster hunter game. I started off with Generations Ultimate (poor entrypoint for the series), and I still consider it my favorite game. That being said, compared to RiseBreak and especially WorldBorne, I prefer Wilds. There are some things I miss from RiseBreak, like switch skills. Many of them were incorporated into the weapons movesets in Wilds, but things like rage slash and guard dash are nowhere to be seen (stalwart guard doesn't count). And being spoiled with hunting styles and hunter arts from the get-go definitely affects my opinion. Overall though, Wilds has a solid 7-9 rating for me, depending on the day.

 I will start by saying I love Monster Hunter Wilds, as someone who played the original on PS2 and then hopped back in to Monster Hunter when World came out since I didn't have most of the Nintendo consoles that the prior entries were on. I've put over 1100 hours in World, significantly less in Rise but that is split across PC and Switch, and now over 300 in Wilds. It is a great game with a ton to do, my personal favorite combat of any Monster Hunter, and great new monsters/monster designs. Capcom has regularly released content as well as optimization fixes (albiet they took their sweet time on the later) and it each update has felt great.

I understand the complaints involving optimization, the game's launch was very buggy, with poor performance, many crashes, and even people with moderate or good pc specs had very unstable gameplay.  I was struggling to get 50 fps at launch, now with some settings tweaks I can get 120 fps easily, with Ray Tracing enabled. I do play on 1080p because I haven't really desired to drop the money for 4k hardware, but the game looks beautiful to me and runs well now. Where improvements like this feel like they should have been available from the start, I still do appreciate when devs don't abandon their games like so many big companies do.

Beyond core gameplay and optimization, I do see a lot of negative reviews for the game not feeling like prior entries. I get that to a degree, and every one is entitled to their own opinion, but I like going in to new series entries with a fresh perspective. They have 100% streamlined monster hunter and made it much less about 'hunting' the mosnter and more about getting straight to the fight. I do miss some of the gathering tracks and the hunts feeling like actual hunts that MH World had, and I think it had a superior design in getting to know your environment while hunting. That being said, there is no denying that the scale and combat in this game is superior, even if I still think of World as my favorite Monster Hunter. It is incredibly addicting to get back to grinding for weapons/armor and playing around with builds. The new updates also took care of difficulty that people complained about and now there's that challenge that World had again. It has me and my friends failing, going back with new builds, and seeing what works again, which is my favorite thing about Monster Hunter games.

Overall, I'd give it a 9/10. It's an excellent addition to the Monster Hunter franchise that just had a rocky start, and has a somewhat mid story, but to be fair, no one plays mainline Monster Hunters for the story.

I bought this game around a month after the release date, knowing how buggy it was during the launch (both server and optimization issues), as there's key available at like 20-25% discount.

I dumped nearly 70-80 in one go. As an old player since PSP day and just catching up with World (I didn't own Rise yet), playing Wilds feels like Capcom finally nailed the problem with the gameplay which was not that player friendly since the old days. It feels more fluid and more like a modern game, especially compared to World. Many quality of life improvement, despite getting criticize from veterans of this game, made it easier for new players to start from this game.

However, that's what the good of this game ended.

Performance issues is pretty well known from the start. Back in 2025, 4060 is quite a capable of GPU even in laptop variant. But even DLSS tech, it can't hold firm even at 60fps stable which is pretty much unacceptable for AAA games in 2025 (quite a norm, yes, but shouldn't be acceptable). The game crashes so many times and nearly toasted my SSD despite just only a couple of months old.

Storywise, I mean they tried to have the story but I think it's so damn boring and doesn't make sense. I think the story in World and Iceborne are more coherent than what Wilds tried to do. I mean if there's a raspberry award for gaming, Wilds would compete with BO7 for the worst storytelling of 2025.

The lack of content also severe. I mean I do remember when World came out there's a looooot of collabs and content that I feel so envious as my previous PC at the time couldn't run World (stable-ly). Wilds feels like it doesn't have any at all. There was probably some plans but got pushed out because of the optimization issues but I think it's just an excuse. There's so many irl collabs with sushi chain and stuff but nearly none in-game content.
Most of "new content" are just giving you some cosmetic stuff by finishing a new quest which took like 30 mins to an hour to finish and we're off to other games/things. I mean you can easily track when there's a "content" update in the game by looking at the player count chart. One oddly spike from the usual player count range, that's the day some content dropped. 

It's not because of it's so much easier than previous games that made the players dropped this game and thirsting of the new content. It's the lack of the communication from the devs/teams that made it feels like Capcom just doesn't give a damn about MonHunt after the launch. I mean you tried to make Wilds a live service thing with stuff you added in the game but didn't bother to commit it all?

And being live-service, I mean at very least just don't be this greedy with paid DLC. Successful live-service games doesn't need this much of cosmetic stuff. I mean people browsing around this page and saw you have like 190 DLCS (with just a few of free DLC) doesn't do much good to you, Capcom. It's good that you giving people choices to buy but I mean you really think people would buy the same decoration just because of different color? Make it a pack and let people customize the color! This is outrageous.

Lastly. This game has a lot of potential. With many of the changes in the gameplay, the one that you can just start any quest, I mean really any quest, by just attacking the monster in the Wilds (hah) a few time is probably one of the thing soooooo many players dreamt of. I just want to put this here that this is the only thing that kept me coming back to this game despite World and Rise runs soooo much better.

Overall. I could only recommend this game if only
1. You really like to hunt monster and didn't care much of how repetitive it is.
2. Decent PC. I wouldn't recommend this game for anyone with GPU under Geforce 2000 series. 16GB of RAM is fine.
3. You have some friends to play with, whether IRL or in-game. It's not that necessary but it's much better to have one.
4. You didn't care much about getting new content bi-weekly  or monthly. If it is, just grab the World + Iceborne or Rise + Sunbreak.

It's called Wilds - but it's not untamed. 

I just start with what this title is not:
Wilds doesn't feature any clever map design, MH World or Iceborne already had: 
- no real verticality. Yes, you have a map with several levels here and there, but they don't feel majestic as in World. 
- no hidden areas. The maps in Wild feel tiny compared to World's structured and layered biomes with secet passages and hidden caves. They don't exist here. 
- Speaking of passages. They call it open world. It's not! Neither can you see adjacent biomes on the horizon, nor are they connected. You have a map, travel to a tunnel, pass through the tunnel, new map. Heck, some even have no tunnels at all, but real loading times as before. 
- No hunts through different biomes. Is that Wild? Or is it just as before? 
- Many beloved Monsters are missing. And there ain't a single epic Elder Dragon. 
- The forest is dense and beautiful. The other maps don't look bad by any means, but they are more like deserts. One with sand, the other with snow and so on. Look at World and you know what you're missing here.
- There are no dynamic events. Weather is changing, that's all. No erupting volcanoes, no flooding, no burning forests... not that I want drama, but it's just not wild at all. Even the snowy landscape from Iceborne had more atmosphere.

Doesn't sound like it so far, but I really like the game. Not the points above and many more, but overall. Especially for players new to the hunting guild, it's a great entrance. Combat is easier to handle and it's actually not that difficult to slay monsters after you get the hang of it. For veterans like me, obviously way too easy at first. Yeah and later. But hey, G-rank, Master Rank ain't here yet. 

To save the game, the devs need to connect the maps. Even more loading tunnels would do as a first step. More monsters, more epicness, more highlights. And a more dynmic and believable, connected world, please. Otherwise it gets boring. 
World had more layers and love in every map and biome. 
And did i even mention that you, the hero hunter/huntress have to sit in a tent all the time? Where is our housing? Where can I watch my caught home pets? Where are my trophies? My style? My spa?? 

Hunting is good. Quality of life features missing. It's wild to think about the fall from World to Wild. Give us more. Give us reason. Give us highlights and spectacle. Surprise us. I'm not gonna farm for pendants.

I'd like to start this off by saying I'm going to try to be pretty transparent about the issues, negatives, and positives of this game - *However* I think the positives far outweigh the negatives. My only real major gripe with the game when it came out was the lack of difficult and engaging content, and bad performance on high-end hardware. Even though the monsters at launch were quite easy, the fights still felt deep and interesting compared to previous titles. Now jumping to the current state of the game, and the game is nearing exactly what I wanted it to be.

My opinions on difficulty:
All the 9* versions of monsters are a blast to fight, with interesting move sets and weaknesses you can exploit at the right times, like any other monster hunter game. Nearly all 9* monsters in this game are much higher quality fights than anything I experienced in either base Rise, World, or even GU. (The only games I've actually put a fair amount of time into). The new monsters and variety of returning monsters from old games and their upgraded move sets and gimmicks are fantastic. Unfortunately if you're a somewhat skilled player, most monsters outside of 9* monsters, don't really put up much of a fight at all. Wounds open instantly and they all get focus strike stun-locked until they die. Unlocking 9* monsters doesn't really take that long in the grand scheme of things and 9* monsters are the endgame and what you should be fighting the most of anyways. Focus Mode makes the combat extremely seamless, although it does remove the aspect of positioning yourself perfectly to land hits. Personally I think Focus Mode should be the future direction of Monster Hunter. Having the pace of the combat be controlled by what I find to be somewhat dated mechanics is just not something I want to see going forward, I want it to feel fresh. I feel as though designing every monster around the hunters' limited control was holding the fights back from ever evolving or changing in any meaningful way, though I can fully understand why people might enjoy the slower paced, more methodical combat of some previous titles. Savage Omega is one of the most unique and interesting fights in a Monster Hunter game to date and nearly forces you to fully utilize all the mechanics Wilds gives you to take it down easily. I will admit, before 9* monsters the game was quite easy, but I really don't understand the difficulty complaints of Wilds. 9* Monsters are both challenging, and fun and rewarding to fight. When a tempered wound pops up on a 9* monster, it actually feels rewarding to focus strike and get that opening, unlike the monsters 8* and below that just become punching bags. Playing through base game GU, Rise, and World, I do not remember a single fight that felt much more difficult or memorable than anything in Wilds, the only thing that actually felt more difficult about going back to those games again after Wilds was the lack of focus mode and trying to re-adjust. If you know how to lock down a monster in one Monster Hunter game, you can do it in any game.

When it comes to performance: 
After the recent performance patch for Steam, the game has become a lot more stable. Personally my FPS didn't *increase* all that much, but the stutters and hitches are basically entirely gone, and it runs a lot smoother.

Overall I have to say the future potential of Wilds, and it's expansion are only looking pretty high upwards. Most of the weapon kits in this game are fun, some could still use some adjustments to flow better. All the monsters are fun and engaging to fight, there isn't too much of a grind but the grind also isn't nonexistent, endgame difficulty is just about right, unique and fun new skills. The only thing the game really lacks right now for me is a couple more 9* versions of some of the existing monsters, a bit more balancing around the main gimmicks of the game (wounds and focus mode), and possibly a bit more options while mounted on a monster than just doing a mounted finisher. (I really liked when you could bonk the monsters into each other lol)

I want to preface the praise I'm about to give this game by stating a couple obvious things. First and foremost, the state the game launched in was appalling. Poor performance across the board, numerous bugs, lack of content, and missing feature were all things that plagued the game upon arrival, which is why I held off on purchasing the game until well after I knew these things had been resolved. Next up, it is absolutely worth mentioning that the game is still not very well optimized. Though playable and mostly smooth, I still experience graphical issues and occasional frame drops, even on my very current hardware. That's not to mention that I can hear my device chugging along whenever I run the game--an issue I have with nothing else I regular play on it. Finally, while I have always been an enjoyer of Monster Hunter campaigns and feel that Wilds is in contention for the very best on that front, the way in which the game railroads you into experiencing that story is heavy-handed to the point of genuine irritation. Again, I did find the story quite compelling, and was hooked for almost every minute of it, but the fact that the game is so restricted until you clear the low rank village questline is absurd. It was frustrating to think about how many people would be put off by an otherwise great game because of how it locks you into experiencing it in one specific way. New players quite literally cannot create an informed opinion on the majority of the game and decide whether or not to refund it because the opening two hours of it are bloated with exposition and tutorials, arguably even more than World was. Additionally, Field Surveys, which are maybe my favorite feature in the game and really allow the world to come to life, are arguably at odds with the campaign. There's so little you can do with them until you've reached the final boss, and you can't meaningfully progress your hunter through them either. Maybe I'm just mourning the old village-hub split, but this game could absolutely benefit from being able to engage with its world, gameplay, and mechanics without being forced into experiencing a slew of story missions which, arguably, don't show this game at its best. Setting aside those blanket criticisms though, I have absolutely adored this game. The new additions, such as seasons, packfights, and seamless traversal between prep and hunting, are the beating heart of this game. Never before has a Monster Hunter world felt so real, so explorable. While I certainly wish there were more reasons to engage with these sprawling natural expanses outside of just hunting, I've found myself so in love with the locals that, more often than not, I'll walk to a destination rather than use the Seikret (this game's equivalent to Rise's palamutes). It feels like a natural evolution of old Monster Hunter's thesis of area design, where each part of a locale has a backdrop which foreshadows the areas to come. For example, the Windward Plains is home to the Wind's Gasp, a gigantic structure which dominates the skyline from almost every vantage point. True to form, rather than simply having this act as set dressing--a skybox which wows the player but offers little more--Wilds allows you to actually travel all the way inside it, just as we once ascended the Ruined Pinnacle in GU or the Ancient Tree in World. Wilds in general has every other series title beat in terms of aesthetics, as even on its lowest settings, this is the best Monster Hunter has ever looked. While I can't say I love how the series has steadily forgone a unique art style in favor of pursuing photorealism, it's hard to deny that the result of that hasn't led to a game wherein every frame is a painting. Even just wandering over a hilltop or quietly observing the endemic life feel breathtaking in a way that is at once bombastic and yet incredibly understated. Everything in this game fills me with a sense of wonder that I struggle to describe, even, or perhaps especially, the mundane. It's a feeling akin to that first time you reach the edge of BoTW's Great Plateau, and are awash with the realization that the giant tutorial area you've just explored, which seemed so expansive from that sweeping title card shot, is actually just a small fraction of the game's world. If I had no care for the health or longevity of my PC, this is a game I would spend countless hours just letting run, checking in every now and again just to glimpse the beautiful world that exists at the players fingertips. Pivoting away from the look of the game, I want to touch on the combat. It is, undeniably, too easy--at least in low rank. While I'm not going to sit here and tell you that low rank Anjanath or Zamtrios were actually secret super bosses in their respective games, I feel that the games which they existed within were simply less streamlined and forgiving. The monster themselves are, across the board, just as challenging, if not more, than they've always been. The drop off in difficulty is instead a result of mechanics like weapon storage, wounds, Seikret fall, and more. Wounds are really the big issue here, as while they make combat undeniably enjoyable, in a sort of glue-eating, braindead way, they cause monsters to crumble like paper, which is a shame considering just how well made almost all of them are. On it's face, I don't think it's a mechanic that's impossible to fix like Iceborne's Clutch Claw was, but I worry that instead of rebalancing the system, the solution to introduce greater difficulty into the game's inevitable Master Rank expansion will be to just overinflate monster healthpools, just like Iceborne did. Regardless of my issues though, I cannot deny just how good combat feels, even with the lack of difficulty. My weapon of choice, hammer, feels even better than it did in World, which for years now has been my gold standard for how the weapon should play and feel. Considering it was maybe the worst weapon to play both in the beta and at launch, this is HUGE praise. I've taken the liberty of trying out some of my other favorites, such as dual blades, Switch Axe, and Light Bow Gun, all of which feel fantastic to play. As mentioned before, the monster are no slouch either, with this game being home to some of the very best fights new gen has to offer, with Rey Dau, Zoh Shia, and Lala Barina being some personal standouts. Ultimately, this game as of writing this review, is a sort of 2 steps forward, 1 step back situation. It introduces a lot of great things to the series, but it almost always comes at the cost of something great, or the introduction of some new, seemingly pointless obstacle. While it's a net positive in terms of the direction it's headed, the many pitfalls it has hold it back from really soaring.
What else is there to say? It's Monster Hunter, but this time it's WILD.

To put it lightly; The Witcher 3 is one of the greatest games ever made. And it, along with its two brilliant expansion packs, is only 10 dollars right now. Don't even hesitate, just try this masterpiece.

Witcher 3 feels like once in a lifetime experience. I bought it in 2017 and played the whole game on Xbox, spent hundreds of hours playing through all the DLCs. I did almost every sidequest, went trough every smallest piece of map, collected every unique piece of special armor set, I almost believed that I am witcher myself (jk).

As a person who read all of the novels and knew almost the whole lore before playing the game, buying this and playing, seeing the things I read about before - felt pretty magical and awesome, truly unique and wholesome experience.

The story is absolutely the best. Even every side-quest feels like an unique story, the most unimportant NPCs have oftentimes the funniest and really interesting lines. 

Playing this game is like watching extremely long movie and being the one who is also in charge of the movie. Stunning graphics, great cutscenes, interesting story, sometimes scary, sometimes funny, sometimes romantic, sometimes just wtf. One of the best aspects is that the whole game is leading to one moment - I do not want to spoiler, but anyone who ever played a game before knows I am talking about a final boss battle - and what makes this truly special is the fact that during this battle, you can literally have or have not the allies based on how you treated certain NPCs and how you interacted or helped some people in the game. You basically are either making valuable allies or not, and that can or can not make a difference during the last battle. 

Another thing, some people claim that combat is lowkey too basic. Well, I cannot agree. You can play with different builds, you can use different potions and different bombs, different spells, wear different armor sets. If you only play the style "hit and dodge, hit and dodge", the combat will obviously get boring soon, but if you use spells, bombs and so on, it is way more interesting and fun.

However, the replayability is really not this game's strength. Even when playing this game makes one of the best gaming memories I ever made during my 28 years on earth, I literally only played this game once. And now, after like 9 years, I am buying it again and will try to recreate the experience on PC instead of Xbox. But, for the last 9 years, I havent felt a smallest urge to replay this game, until now. This doesnt mean that you shouldnt buy the game and try it - I absolutely encourage you to try it. I am just saying that, for me, playing this once per a decade felt enough.

If I had to give this game a certain points, I would give this 10/10. Just because the replayability is not high for me, doesnt mean the game isn't great. 

Oh and dont get me started to talk about GWENT... I was disregarding GWENT for like first 100 hours of gameplay, until I tried it once and fell in love so hard I cannot even describe.

Seriously, if you like RPGs, medieval themes and bit of magic, this game is absolute beast.

Easily one of the best and most immersive RPG's released in the last few generations. The world feels alive, the story is solid, the side quests are generally great and the DLC's are amazing. You'll often find yourself in morally ambiguous situations that make you question your own values as well as the situations outcome.

For some the combat is considered pretty weak; however, I personally find it suits the game well. There is a standard and heavy attack, dodging and parrying. You can also mix in a few small witcher spells and bombs. There is also the option to play on higher difficulties, where managing your resources and planning ahead becomes much more critical as you need to adapt and exploit your enemies weaknesses; great if you're looking for an additional challenge.

Overall I'd still consider this amazing game one of the best out there today.
